gist: US death row inmate Christa Pike is unconscious after a failed lethal injection execution.
Lawyers claim prison officials botched the execution by failing to insert IV lines correctly.
Tennessee's governor ordered an independent review and halted all executions for the year.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: US death row inmate Christa Pike is unconscious and on a ventilator following a failed execution attempt. Her lawyers filed an emergency motion to preserve evidence, alleging prison officials botched the lethal injection. They state officials used at least seven needles, bending one, while Pike whimpered and cried. An expert suggested the drug pentobarbital entered tissue under her skin rather than her bloodstream due to ruptured veins or blood clots.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has halted all executions in the state for the year and ordered an independent review. Pike's lawyers had previously warned that her blood-clotting condition and small veins risked causing unnecessary pain.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Authorities have not yet said whether they will attempt to execute Pike again, and her lawyers are seeking to preserve all physical, written, and electronic evidence.

sections.text: The separatist Parti Québécois, led by Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, is projected to win a minority government in Quebec's provincial election. This marks the party's first time in power since 2014, following the collapse of the Coalition Avenir Québec.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Daniil Medvedev was disqualified from his China Open semi-final against Novak Djokovic after hitting a spectator in the face with a ball. Trailing in the second set, Medvedev swiped at a ball in annoyance after it ricocheted off the back of the court. The ball hit a front-row spectator, who was helped out of the arena. Following discussions with the umpire and an ATP official, Medvedev was disqualified.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Defaults in tennis are rare and occur for code of conduct violations. Although players typically receive multiple warnings before disqualification, Medvedev's offence was severe enough for an instant default. Consequently, he loses his ranking points and prize money from Beijing. The incident highlights ongoing concerns regarding his on-court temper and emotional control.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Astronomers reviewing archive data from the Hubble Space Telescope identified unrecognised chemical features in the white dwarf star HS 0209+0832. Using updated databases, researchers matched these features to niobium, indicating the presence of a second-generation planet formed from ejected stellar material.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: This discovery suggests that planetary systems can form around stellar remnants after a star dies, opening a new chapter in the study of planetary evolution.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Researchers plan to use the Hubble Space Telescope for the next several years to explore how common these second-generation planets are.

timeline.text: Prisoner took his own life after terror order had 'substantial impact' on mental state, inquest finds

gist: An inquest found terror control measures substantially impacted a prisoner's mental state before death.
Akhtar Uddin died in HMP Wandsworth after being jailed for breaching a TPIM order.
The coroner will issue a report over concerns regarding risks to TPIM subjects.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Akhtar Uddin died in HMP Wandsworth on Christmas Day 2021 whilst serving a sentence for breaching a Terrorism Prevention and Investigation Measure (TPIM). An inquest jury at Inner West London Coroner's Court concluded the restrictive order and fears over its reimposition had a substantial impact on his mental state. They also found the prison service failed to provide the support he needed. Jurors noted it was not possible to determine if he intended his death.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: This was the first inquest to consider the impact of TPIMs. Evidence revealed prison staff had little awareness of the restrictions, leading to unintentionally cruel treatment. The coroner noted the state assessed the risk Uddin posed to others, but not risks to Uddin himself, highlighting a broader lack of support for subjects.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Coroner Bernard Richmond KC stated he will issue a preventing future deaths report to the government because of concerns about risks to others subjected to terrorism control measures.

fivew: An inquest jury concluded that a terrorism control order substantially affected a prisoner's mental state before he took his own life.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Perseverance explored Lac de Charmes beyond Jezero crater's western rim and found a vast field of light-toned rocks. The rover has been investigating their composition, indicating they are gabbro formed deep in the crust, and examining a patch of possible breccia bedrock.

sections.heading: Why it matters

gist: Cooler air, cloud and rain will sweep across the UK from Tuesday.
Temperatures will drop into the mid-teens, ending weeks of unusually warm conditions.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Cooler air, rain and strong winds are sweeping across the UK from the north-west. Temperatures are falling from the low 20s to the mid-teens, with Wednesday expected to be the first day since 11 June without 20C recorded anywhere in the country.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Although mid-teen temperatures are normal for early October, the contrast with recent unusually warm weather makes the change feel particularly dramatic.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Thursday will start chilly with mist, fog and rural frost before sunshine emerges under temporary high pressure. Atlantic systems will bring further rain and wind on Friday, before temperatures recover towards average at the weekend.

gist: Caleb Flynn received a life sentence for murdering his wife, Ashley Flynn.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Caleb Flynn was sentenced to life in prison without parole after being convicted of murdering his wife, Ashley Flynn. Prosecutors said he shot her in February at their home in Tipp City and staged a fake burglary to cover it up. He was also convicted of tampering with evidence and other charges. During the trial, evidence included text messages to his former mistress and device activity contradicting his claim that he was asleep.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The case exposed a premeditated murder linked to an affair with a church intern. Letters from the couple's daughters and statements from family members detailed the profound emotional devastation caused by the crime. The judge described Flynn as an extreme risk to the public.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Flynn's lawyer stated an intention to file a notice of appeal, arguing a lack of evidence regarding prior calculation and design.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Care proceedings for infants in England have risen by 64% over two decades. Experts warn many babies are taken into care because struggling families lack adequate support.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Most adoptions of infants occur without the written consent of their birth parents. Since early intervention funding has fallen by 44% over a decade, borderline cases are increasingly entering the care system, risking permanent, unnecessary family separations.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: New guidance to reduce short-notice care hearings for newborns will be announced by the end of the year. Additionally, the government is investing £2.4bn to improve early support for families.

gist: Canadian veterans and families express anger over recent critical remarks about their military from US figures.
Donald Trump, JD Vance, and other US officials made disparaging comments regarding Canada's defence and contributions.
The remarks have strained diplomatic relations and upset veterans who served alongside US troops.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: US vice-president JD Vance commented that Canada underinvested in its military. Donald Trump's transportation secretary Sean Duffy stated Canada does not have a military, while Pete Hegseth mocked Canadian cadets and a coast guard detachment. Trump previously claimed Canadian and Nato forces in Afghanistan were never needed. Canadian veterans and families condemned these remarks as disrespectful.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The remarks sparked a diplomatic dispute, deeply angering Canadian veterans who fought alongside US troops in Afghanistan and lost comrades. Veterans feel betrayed by the ungrateful attitude after years of close military cooperation.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Some US politicians have attempted to make amends, such as Arizona Democrat senator Rueben Gallego travelling to Ottawa to call the tweets deeply disrespectful. Meanwhile, Canadian veterans are reconsidering their personal ties and future support for the United States.

fivew: Canadian veterans such as Perry Chalmers and Chris Banks, alongside US figures like JD Vance and Donald Trump.
Canadian veterans and families expressed anger after Donald Trump and US allies made disparaging remarks about the Canadian military.
Recently, following comments made by US officials and earlier remarks by Donald Trump.
Veterans feel deeply insulted and betrayed by US criticism after decades of joint military sacrifice and cooperation.

quotes.text: To hear him spit on our sacrifice is insulting, it’s hurtful, and it’s disrespectful to the dead.

timeline.text: US households pay 62% more for water than they did a decade ago, study finds

gist: US households pay 62% more for drinking water than a decade ago.
Water prices rose significantly faster than overall inflation, groceries, and incomes.
Corporate-owned water systems charged substantially higher average annual rates than public systems.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A study by Food & Water Watch found that US household drinking water bills increased by 62% over the past decade. The average household using 60,000 gallons paid $531 in 2025. Costs varied greatly by state and ownership, with corporate-owned utilities charging significantly more than publicly owned systems.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Water costs rose faster than inflation, grocery prices, and median household incomes, hitting low-income households the hardest. Experts cited ageing infrastructure, regulatory compliance, and climate change as key cost drivers.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Organizations highlighted the need for infrastructure updates, local affordability programs, and federal support to prevent vulnerable communities from facing severe financial burdens or compromised water safety.

fivew: Food & Water Watch and US households.

gist: Ofcom is investigating Meta over Instagram's Instants feature under UK safety laws.
The regulator claims Meta failed to conduct proper risk assessments before launching the tool.
Meta insists it conducted a risk analysis and briefed Ofcom before the launch.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Ofcom is investigating Meta for potentially breaching the UK's Online Safety Act. The regulator claims Meta failed to carry out adequate risk assessments regarding illegal content and children's safety before launching Instagram's "Instants" feature in May. Meta states it conducted a risk analysis and briefed Ofcom multiple times before the launch.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Under the Online Safety Act, tech firms must assess risks before launching significant platform changes. Failing to comply can result in formal warnings or fines of up to 10% of global revenue. Meta is already facing other investigations and is legally challenging Ofcom over fees and information demands.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Ofcom's probe will examine if Meta breached its duties. Meta has stated it will co-operate with the investigation.

fivew: The communications regulator Ofcom and tech company Meta.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Russian drone attacks targeting Ukrainian passenger trains have escalated. Passengers describe emergency evacuations, waiting in the dark near explosions, and long delays. sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The attacks disrupt vital transport that has kept Ukraine running since the full-scale invasion, putting passengers and crew members at risk. Russia's defence ministry states it targets infrastructure used for military transport, while the railway operator prioritises passenger safety amid increasingly sophisticated drone technology.

sections.heading: What happens next

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Counter-terror police arrested a 22-year-old British national in Westminster on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. This marked the seventh arrest linked to a 27 September incident near RAF Fairford involving suspicious vehicles. All previously detained suspects were released on bail, and no charges have been brought.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: RAF Fairford has been used by the US Air Force for defensive Middle East strikes against Iran. Following threats, the US recently removed its bombers from the base. Tensions have risen since Iran's Revolutionary Guards designated the base a legitimate target, though Iran denies any involvement.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Police stated the investigation remains live as specialist teams pursue multiple lines of inquiry. US European Command said it will continue assessing the threat environment at bases.

sections.text: Paramount Skydance completed its $110bn merger with Warner Bros Discovery, uniting Hollywood powerhouses and major franchises into a single entertainment behemoth named Skydance.

sections.text: Subscribers may face higher streaming prices due to massive debt and combined platforms. The deal also threatens thousands of jobs in the film and TV industry, while raising questions about newsroom independence at CNN and CBS.

gist: Tobias Rausch became the first far-right regional speaker in Germany since World War Two.
The AfD candidate won the vote in Saxony-Anhalt with support from outside his party.
Other parties expressed alarm over the breaking of the political firewall against the far right.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Tobias Rausch of the AfD was elected as the speaker of the Saxony-Anhalt regional parliament. He secured enough votes in the secret ballot with backing from members of other parties, including the BSW. Hans-Thomas Tillschneider was also chosen as his deputy later in the day.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: This event marks the first time a far-right party has secured the speaker position in a German regional parliament since the second world war. It signals a breakdown of the political firewall that previously isolated the AfD, raising concerns among opposition politicians and observers about the normalisation of far-right influence.

gist: Trinidad and Tobago passed the Special Operations Bill 2026 to tackle high crime.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The government passed the Special Operations Bill 2026 on 24 September to tackle high crime and murder rates. Journalists raised an outcry because the legislation boosts police powers of search and seizure without explicitly naming journalism as a protected lawful trade.

sections.text: Media workers fear the sweeping powers allow police to search and seize devices, threatening their ability to protect confidential sources and whistleblowers. Critics also point to declining access to government officials and rising communication interception warrants.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Home Office officers arrested two people in London on suspicion of fraud and immigration offences, while a third person was arrested for being in the country illegally. Officials seized phones, jewellery and cash. Investigations revealed a criminal network linked to a Bangladeshi community LGBT organisation called Apanjon charged migrants between £1,000 and £4,500 for fake letters, staged photographs and fabricated relationship evidence.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The Home Office is reviewing more than 100 asylum claims linked to the criminal network, admitting some fraudulent applications would have undoubtedly been granted. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood condemned the fraudsters for mocking real victims, warning that cheats will have their claims thrown out and be removed from the country.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The Home Office is continuing its review of asylum claims linked to both the Apanjon network and previous reporting involving Worcester LGBT. Perpetrators face prosecution, confiscation of assets, and a maximum sentence of up to 10 years in prison for asylum fraud.

gist: Families of missing flood victims in Nepal struggle to obtain death certificates.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A deadly flood tore through the China-Nepal border, leaving more than 5,000 people missing and thousands of buildings destroyed. Because many bodies cannot be recovered, families are performing symbolic funerals using sacred grass. However, under Nepal's civil code, missing persons are only presumed dead after 12 years, preventing relatives from obtaining death certificates.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Without death certificates, families cannot access bereavement compensation and funeral funds needed to rebuild their lives. Local officials say everything is on hold due to outdated laws meant for people who travelled abroad, creating an administrative nightmare.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Local governments are urging the prime minister's office to resolve the death confirmation issue. The home ministry stated the government is ready to amend the law if required, while prime minister Balen Shah pushes for international grant-based support to aid reconstruction.

gist: Kemi Badenoch will declare a looming battle of ideas against Labour in British politics.
The Conservatives seek to re-frame their image following their 2024 general election defeat.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch is set to address her party's annual conference in Birmingham, framing the upcoming contest against Labour as a battle for the soul of the nation. The Conservatives have unveiled proposals including a £10bn UK air defence system and halving employer National Insurance contributions for workers aged 21 to 24 to 7.5%. Speculation also surrounds potential cuts to inheritance tax, with the shadow chancellor reviewing options.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The Conservatives are trailing both Labour and Reform UK in opinion polls and are attempting to rebuild public support after their 2024 general election defeat. Badenoch argues Labour's approach will bring higher taxes, while Labour responded that the Conservatives completely failed to grow the economy during their 14 years in office.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The party will publish its funding plan for the £2.3bn National Insurance policy on Wednesday, while Chancellor John Healey prepares to deliver the government's Budget on 28 October.

sections.text: UK house prices showed no growth in September, remaining similar to previous levels. This followed a decline in August. Extreme conditions have forced medical staff to perform surgeries using phone torches.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Russian forces have stripped hospitals in occupied Ukrainian territories of equipment, medicine, and furniture, redirecting resources to their military. Many experienced medical staff have fled. Patients face severe shortages, with some surgeries performed without anaesthesia or using mobile phone torches for light.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The lack of resources and staff has led to rising maternal and child mortality rates. Furthermore, Russia's passportisation policy means medical services are denied to those without Russian passports and compulsory health insurance. Curfews and blockades also prevent patients from reaching emergency care.

gist: Police in England and Wales routinely fail to investigate image-based abuse, research shows.
A super-complaint has been launched following extremely low prosecution rates for these crimes.
Victims face inappropriate comments and are often forced to gather their own evidence.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Campaigners have filed a super-complaint against police forces in England and Wales. Research involving 100 victims revealed that officers routinely fail to investigate image-based abuse, with some dismissing reports or making inappropriate comments.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Despite rising public awareness, charging rates remain extremely low, averaging just 4.5% last year. Victims, who are overwhelmingly female, are often left to gather their own evidence, causing further distress.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The College of Policing alongside the Independent Office for Police Conduct will assess the complaint to decide whether to launch a broader investigation.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Stephen King has published 'Other Worlds Than These', the final volume in the fantasy trilogy that began with 'The Talisman' in 1984. sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: A review in The Guardian describes the 800-plus-page novel as self-indulgent, repetitive and boring. While it offers moments of joy for dedicated Stephen King fans, the reviewer argues it is not vintage King and cannot be recommended to general readers.

timeline.text: Chemistry Nobel awarded for solving mystery of life's asymmetry
Nobel prize in chemistry awarded for work on mirror-image molecules

gist: Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Chemistry Nobel Prize.
They solved the century-old mystery of life's molecular asymmetry, known as chirality.
Their work allows chemical reactions to produce specific mirror-image molecule forms.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai for solving the mystery of life's asymmetry. Kagan discovered a new way of manipulating chemical reactions in 1986, and Soai developed a reaction in 1995 and 2003 that could produce only the desired version of an organic molecule.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Living organisms exclusively function with one version of mirror-image molecules, a property called chirality. Understanding how to control this is crucial for making effective medicines, as different versions of chiral drug molecules can have entirely different biological effects, such as the toxic versus effective forms seen in thalidomide.

fivew: French scientist Henri B. Kagan and Japan's Kenso Soai
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded for discoveries explaining molecular chirality and asymmetric synthesis.
To recognize their solution to the chemical mystery of life's asymmetry.

quotes.text: This is one of the most exciting days of my life.
Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old

sections.text: At least 24 people died in overnight strikes across Ukraine, including an apartment block in Pryluky where 18 people were killed. Attacks also hit Kyiv, Dnipro, Kremenchuk, Zaporizhzhia and Oleksandriya. Meanwhile, ships were attacked in the Black Sea.

articles.title: World’s largest penguin colony suffers ‘enormous population crash’
articles.standfirst: Chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski Island in Antarctica down by two-thirds since 2011, probably due to climate crisis

timeline.text: World's largest penguin colony hit by 'alarming' decline in numbers

gist: Almost two-thirds of chinstrap penguins disappeared from Zavodovski Island between 2011 and 2025.
Scientists attribute the alarming decline to climate change shifting krill populations southwards.
Macaroni penguins on the same island increased in number due to their broader diet.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Aerial surveys and tracking studies revealed a 63% decline in occupied chinstrap penguin nests on Zavodovski Island between 2011 and 2025. This loss means the island has lost its title as home to the world's largest penguin colony. While chinstrap numbers crashed, macaroni penguin populations on the same island increased.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Researchers state that climate disruption is warming waters and pushing krill southwards, leaving specialist chinstraps struggling to find food. Scientists warn that this enormous population crash risks wider ecosystem collapse.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The rapid decline of chinstrap penguins may lead to the species being officially classified as endangered.

fivew: Researchers from the British Antarctic Survey.
Almost two-thirds of chinstrap penguins disappeared from their colony.
Climate change warmed ocean waters and caused their food supply to move.

quotes.text: It is an enormous population crash, equivalent to half a million breeding individuals being lost from that island

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Wittington Investments agreed to buy Boots in a $8.9bn (£6.7bn to £6.74bn) deal from Sycamore Partners and the Pessina family. sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Boots has faced uncertain ownership and closed hundreds of branches. The new owners plan shop upgrades and healthcare service expansions, ending a period where ownership changed with extraordinary frequency.

sections.heading: What happens next

sections.text: Online figures on social media tried to reveal the identity of a Cornell University student suing fraternity members for rape. Commentators shared details and names, leading to abuse directed at several women wrongly identified as the plaintiff.

sections.text: The targeted harassment shows how survivor privacy remains under threat on open platforms. Experts warn that exposing plaintiffs deters victims of sexual violence from reporting crimes or seeking legal recourse.

gist: Labour faces the worst parliament for living standards since 1961, a study warns.
Rising energy and housing costs threaten household incomes without bold policy action.
The budget may offer limited support, though experts urge more ambitious measures.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A Joseph Rowntree Foundation analysis predicts average household incomes after housing costs will fall by £440 to £770 by 2029-30. Rising energy and housing costs, exacerbated by conflict in the Middle East and higher mortgage rates, are driving the squeeze.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Millions of families risk going without essentials like food and basic toiletries unless the government takes bold policy action.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Cabinet taskforces are working on cost of living measures for a 10-year plan this autumn, while a budget is expected soon with potential increases to the warm homes discount.

fivew: A study warns Labour could oversee the worst parliament on record for living standards.
Three weeks ahead of the budget.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Canada indefinitely paused plans to expand assisted dying to individuals whose sole condition is mental illness. Justice Minister Sean Fraser stated the government will introduce a law to suspend the expansion.

gist: Four Conservative candidates have declared their run for the London mayoral nomination.

The final shortlist of two candidates is expected to be announced in November.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Four Conservative candidates have declared their bids to run for London mayor in the May 2028 election. The declared runners are Sir James Cleverly, Festus Akinbusoye, Andrew Boff, and Alex Challoner.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The Conservatives have only won the London mayoralty once in 26 years, with Boris Johnson. Since then, they have lost three consecutive elections to Labour's Sadiq Khan. However, the party hopes to regain ground following local election victories in Westminster and Wandsworth in May 2026.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The hopefuls must wait until November to see if they make the final shortlist. London party members are expected to choose between the final two candidates, who will likely be announced on 20 November.

gist: JJ Gabriel featured in Manchester United's team photo despite his desire to leave.
The teenager decided to seek a departure after missing a Champions League match.
Manchester United still hold his registration amid interest from top European clubs.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: JJ Gabriel was included in Manchester United's official senior team photograph, taken on 8 September. Two days later, he played his final match for the club and announced his intention to leave. His decision followed his omission from Michael Carrick's squad for a Champions League fixture against Sabah FK.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Gabriel is now pursued by leading European sides, including Real Madrid and Barcelona. Manchester United maintain they demonstrated commitment to the forward by providing first-team care, regular access to senior staff, and lobbying the Premier League regarding his shirt name.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: United still hold Gabriel's registration and have attempted to reconcile with him. The club would consider legal action if evidence of illegal inducement by another club or agent emerges.

gist: Scotland lost two to one against Slovenia at Hampden.
New boss Sebastien Pocognoli faced sharp criticism after the dismal display.
The defeat put Scotland's bid for second place in jeopardy.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Scotland suffered a one-two defeat against Slovenia at Hampden on a dismal night. Slovenia carved out numerous chances, exploiting vast spaces in midfield and at the back. Ryan Christie scored for Scotland, but defensive frailties allowed Aljosa Matko and Danijel Sturm to secure a deserved victory for the visitors.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The damaging defeat threatens Scotland's bid for second place in their Nations League group and a favourable pot two seeding for December's Euros draw. It undermined the recent positivity surrounding the team and brought an abrupt end to manager Sebastien Pocognoli's honeymoon period.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Head coach Sebastien Pocognoli must nurse his wounds, evaluate his players, and drill his message into the squad. Scotland face their next fixtures in November, playing away against Switzerland and at home against North Macedonia with no real margin for error.

fivew: Scotland's football team managed by Sebastien Pocognoli and Slovenia.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Jon Rahm is set to leave LIV Golf because he considers the terms of LIV 2.0 unacceptable. LIV Golf filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the United States in September following the withdrawal of Saudi Arabia's funding. The league has secured possible financing from BC Partners Credit for the 2027 season. Rahm and LIV representatives are in advanced discussions for a consensual separation agreement.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Rahm is owed an unsecured claim of $7.5m, making him the top creditor among the 30 largest unsecured claims. Participants are owed at least $45m and can leave, as players have no obligation to sign on to LIV 2.0.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Talks are open until 25 October, and it is hoped that a consensual separation agreement will be finalised by a court hearing on 5 November.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Sir Richard expressed hope that Manchester does not lose UAE investment, noting he would be concerned if it stopped.

Why is JJ Gabriel in Man Utd's team photo?

gist: JJ Gabriel features in Manchester United's official team photo despite efforts to leave.
Europe's top clubs are interested in the teenager as he holds a European Union passport.
His decision to seek a move was triggered by non-inclusion against Sabah FK.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: JJ Gabriel is included in Manchester United's official team photo for the season. The pictures were taken before he informed the club of his intention to leave. His exit decision was triggered by not being included in the squad to face Sabah FK.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Gabriel is a target for several top European clubs, including Real Madrid and Barcelona. Manchester United hold his registration and would consider legal action if illegal inducement emerges.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Gabriel is set to turn 16 and his next involvement in a United game will virtually certainly be as an opposition player.
